Rank your personal values, two at a time

Most values exercises ask you to sort thirty words into order in one go. Choosing which of two matters more is easier and more honest, and enough of those choices give you the order.

Why picking pairs works here

  • Edit the list before you start: add values that matter to you and delete ones that don't. Twelve to twenty works well.
  • The result marks places your answers did not settle, so you can see which values you genuinely hold equal rather than forcing a tie-break.
  • Nothing is uploaded or stored anywhere but your browser. Close the tab and it's gone.

What it doesn't do: It's a reflection exercise, not a psychological assessment. A ranking from a few dozen picks is an estimate, and how you answer can change with your mood that day.

Compared with what you'd use today

Card-sort worksheets, paid values assessments, or a coach. A worksheet makes you hold the whole list in your head; this asks one small question at a time.

Under the hood: a Bradley-Terry model refit after every answer, an adaptive question picker, and a stop rule checked against simulated respondents, including ones whose picks are close calls. The method and its measurements.
